content.comment_body: We have used modules with article numbers ranging from [article_no] to [article_no]. Recently, we encountered a significant issue when upgrading from [version_no] to [version_no]: inputs 1 and 2 on the newer hardware are much more sensitive. For instance, on [article_no], an input required about 6800 ohms or less to activate, but on [article_no], inputs 1 and 2 activate at 47000 ohms. This has caused problems at one of our installation sites. I recall reading that inputs 1 and 2 are high speed inputs—could this sensitivity be a settings issue? As a temporary fix, we're avoiding the use of inputs 1 and 2, but sometimes all 8 inputs are needed. Using shielded wire isn't feasible for us, as we don’t control the wire type used. Wire runs are typically 12 feet, occasionally up to 100 feet. Thanks for any advice. [user_name]

On [article_no], an input required about 6800 ohms or less, but on [article_no], inputs 1 and 2 activate at 47000 ohms. Hello! I imagine you’re using a variable resistor or voltage divider to detect a digital stage—could you explain your setup a bit more or clarify how the resistance change is affecting your system?

We're just using a push button switch at the end of 12-100 feet of wire. The newer module is giving us false input signals when the switch isn't pressed. When the site tech disconnected and reconnected the wires, the system assumed the input was triggered and executed the program. I suspected the input impedance changed between versions, so I checked the resistance threshold at which the inputs activate. Not every installation uses a mechanical switch; sometimes we use a solid-state relay, which could also trigger problems if the off-state resistance is 47000 ohms. 47000 ohms wasn’t the highest tested; it’s just where I stopped for now—more testing will be done Friday/Saturday. The issue is only present with inputs 1 and 2 so far. I've noticed that inputs 1 and 2 are also AI3 and AI4 on this version, which is new. Regarding our application: the system sequences unlocking/opening a pedestrian doorway, operated by a push button inside and card reader outside. Thanks. [user_name]

I’ve identified the issue—the hardware model has changed. We're using the 12/24RC version. In [article_no], I1-I6 require 1.5mA for high status, while I7 and I8 require 0.1mA. In [article_no], I3-I6 need 2mA for high status; I1, I2, I7, and I8 need 0.15mA. Previously, using I1-I6 avoided this issue, but that's no longer possible. Because we don't use shielded wire, the cable is likely picking up stray voltage or current, triggering the now more-sensitive inputs. Thanks for reviewing. [user_name]

Hello all. The inputs in the [version_no] models have been updated for 12/24 RC & RCo as well as for [product_name] 24 & 24o devices. I1 & I2 can now optionally accept 0..10V analog signals (AI3 & AI4), so input current sensitivity was likely altered for analog-to-digital conversion. Inputs I3-I6 also changed—these are now high-speed counters up to 5kHz instead of just I5 and I6 as before, so their sensitivity may differ as well. The detection threshold for HI or LO status is more driven by voltage than current. This situation demonstrates why high-quality shielded cable is essential in industrial environments with longer wiring or nearby switching devices—unwanted signals are easily picked up! Good to see progress and practical solutions.

Hello! One workaround is to add a relay at the input—electrical noise typically won't trigger a relay, but a legitimate ON signal will. That's one option for solving this issue. Does anyone have additional suggestions?
Another possible solution is to add a pull-down resistor to keep the signal reliably low.

Update: Shielded wire is now required based on test results. I laid out 100 feet of 18 AWG lamp wire on the shop floor, which stored enough charge to trigger inputs 1 and 2, but not 3 through 6. As another user suggested, adding a pull-down resistor (we’re using 4700 ohms) aligns the input impedance with other channels. I currently have 50 units in the shop and was worried for a couple days, but this fix is inexpensive—looks like it will be a good weekend.
Using a relay would be much more reliable. Hope this solution works for you.

I had a client who used Honeywell HOA0892-T55 transmissive sensors (slotted photointerrupters) with all 8 inputs of the controller. The output phototransistors could sink about 1.4mA. Using 8.2K ohm pull-ups on I1, I2, I7, and I8 was effective, giving logic levels of 0.26V (low) and 10.8V (high). But with the high-speed inputs (I3-I6), the sensor output couldn’t reach above about 5.5V, behaving as if [article_no] has a 5860 ohm input resistance to common. Since our sensor signals are inherently low-speed, a simple quad op-amp (LM324) with RF/noise filter and 100 ohm series resistors to I3-I6 solved the problem. The manual describes different input current requirements by pin, but elsewhere input impedance is shown as 80K ohms per input (72K ohms when enabled as analog), and it would be helpful if input loading values were clarified. This would give users a clearer path for reconciling resistor values needed for consistent logic levels.

analysis.insight_summary: Users experienced unexpected changes in input sensitivity between hardware revisions, resulting in false digital input activation and compromised reliability. The sudden change disrupted installations and caused confusion, especially given that documentation didn’t adequately clarify input current thresholds, analog configuration, or practical wiring/loading guidance. The large number of affected units amplified the urgency for quick fixes, leading to ad-hoc solutions like pull-down resistors or relays. Documentation gaps were specifically noted regarding input behaviors and recommended cabling practices.
analysis.user_expectations: Users expect hardware updates to maintain compatibility and avoid unexpected changes in input operation. They want comprehensive, clear documentation detailing input characteristics, current/voltage thresholds, analog options, and recommended wiring setups to enable reliable system design in various environments.
